answer:
The landlord is partly right, but "no matter what" overstates it. Your lease has no early-termination clause, so the question is what Florida law lets the landlord do when you leave early.

**What the law says (§ 83.595).** If you surrender or abandon the apartment, the landlord must choose one of these options:
- **(1)** Treat the lease as ended, which ends your liability.
- **(2)** Retake the apartment for your account and re-rent it. You would owe only the difference between your rent and what the landlord gets from re-renting. The landlord must make a good-faith effort to re-rent, and any rent received from a new tenant is deducted from what you owe.
- **(3)** "Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due."
- **(4)** Charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee, but only if you signed a separate addendum agreeing to it when the lease was made. The fee can't exceed 2 months' rent.

**Applied to your lease.**
- Option (4) doesn't appear to be available. The lease I have is ten numbered sections. None sets a fee or liquidated damages, and there is no addendum. Section 10 says the lease is the whole agreement. If you signed a separate addendum that isn't in what I have, that would change this.
- Option (3) is the landlord's strongest position. If the landlord stands by, you would owe rent as it comes due through July 31, 2026, which is what the manager is saying. Nothing in the lease or the statute lets you end the lease early on your own.
- Option (2) is your best protection. If the landlord retakes the apartment and re-rents it, the landlord must make a good-faith effort, and the new tenant's rent reduces what you owe. The manager's statement doesn't rule this out, because you would still owe rent for any months the apartment stays empty.
- The statute says the landlord has a duty to re-rent only under option (2), when the landlord retakes the apartment. It doesn't say which option applies when the landlord won't say what it is doing. The landlord could read "rent through July" as option (3), which has no duty to re-rent. You could argue the landlord is retaking the apartment, which would trigger the duty. The statute doesn't settle which reading is right.

Did the manager's reply say anything about trying to re-rent the apartment after you leave?

tool_calls.result: 83.595 Choice of remedies upon breach or early termination by tenant. — If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may: (1) Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant; (2) Retake possession of the dwelling unit for the account of the tenant, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting. If the landlord retakes possession, the landlord has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises, and any rent received by the landlord as a result of the reletting must be deducted from the balance of rent due from the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, the term “good faith in attempting to relet the premises” means that the landlord uses at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units but does not require the landlord to give a preference in renting the premises over other vacant dwelling units that the landlord owns or has the responsibility to rent; (3) Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due; or (4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit. (b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 . History. — s. 2, ch. 87-369; s. 4, ch. 88-379; s. 448, ch. 95-147; s. 2, ch. 2008-131.

You should object to the $500 claim in writing, and do it soon. Don't wait to see whether the landlord sends the rest.

**Why this applies to you.** You confirmed this isn't school housing, so Fla. Stat. ch. 83, part II covers your rental. Your lease ran to July 31, 2026. You moved out July 30 and the landlord sent a claim notice, so the objection rules apply.

**What the statute says about objecting.** Under 83.49(3)(b), if you don't object "within 15 days after receipt of the landlord's notice of intention to impose a claim," the landlord may deduct the claim. The landlord must then send you the balance within 30 days after the date on the notice. Your objection should go in writing to the address the notice gives for it. Keep a copy and proof of how you sent it.

If you miss the 15 days, you don't lose everything. Under 83.49(3)(b), a late objection doesn't waive your right to sue separately. Objecting on time is still the safer course.

**Two things I can't settle yet.**
1. **Whether the landlord's notice was proper.** 83.49(3)(a) requires the notice within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, and by certified mail to your last known mailing address. It can go by e-mail only if you both signed an e-mail addendum. Your lease says in §8 that you "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail," and an addendum is the only other way. The 30 days haven't run out either way. Counted from the lease end, they run through 2026-08-30. Counted from your move-out, they run through 2026-08-29. So the notice isn't late. It could still be defective if it came some other way, such as regular mail or hand delivery.
   - **If it was defective:** you can argue the landlord forfeited the claim and owes you the full $1,050. The statute says a landlord who fails to give the required notice "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit." The landlord could still sue you for damages afterward.
   - **If it counts anyway:** the other reading is that a notice you actually received in time is enough. That rests on 83.505(6), which says it "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." Then the objection process above governs.
2. **Your objection deadline.** I've noted that you received the letter today, 2026-08-20. Please confirm that date in the sidebar. I can only count your 15 days once it's confirmed.

**Carpet cleaning.** The lease doesn't mention carpet cleaning or any cleaning charge. §6 only says to leave the apartment "clean and empty." Your objection can say the charge is not justified, and you can ask for an itemized basis.

If this goes to court, 83.49(3)(c) gives the winning side its court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
Landlord didn't come Thursday, so he broke his own promise. That alone doesn't let you break the lease or stop paying rent. Those remedies depend on a written notice, and I don't think the 7-day clock has started yet.

**What the statute requires**
- To terminate, you must give the landlord a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to terminate. He then has 7 days to fix it. If he doesn't, you may terminate. (§ 83.56(1))
- To withhold rent, you need the same kind of notice, saying you intend not to pay rent. After 7 days, the failure to repair can be a defense if he sues you for nonpayment. (§ 83.60(1)(b)) If he sues, you would also have to pay the rent into the court registry while the case runs. (§ 83.60(2))
- Both remedies cover only a material failure to comply with § 83.51(1).

**Why the clock probably hasn't started**
- You told me you texted him on April 11. I don't know whether the text said you intended to terminate or withhold rent. If it only reported the broken AC, it wasn't the notice these sections describe.
- Even if it did say that, a text isn't a delivery method the statute lists. The listed methods are mailing, delivering a copy, leaving a copy at the residence if the tenant is absent, or e-mail under § 83.505. (§ 83.56(4)) E-mail under § 83.505 requires a signed addendum, and your lease says you "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail." (Lease § 8)
- Your lease says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or "sent there by certified mail." (Lease § 7)
- The count_days tool puts 7 days after April 11 at April 18, which is today. That only helps you if the text was a valid notice with the required statement, and I doubt it was.

**Whether AC is covered at all**
- Section 83.51(1) requires the landlord to comply with applicable building, housing, and health codes. The specific list in § 83.51(2)(a) names heat in winter, not cooling.
- If a Gainesville code requires working cooling, the AC outage could be a § 83.51(1) violation. That is something you would have to check. If no code does, § 83.51 may not reach it. Then you'd be relying on "material provisions of the rental agreement," and your lease has no clause about AC or repairs. Both readings are open.

**What to do**
- Keep paying rent on time for now. Rent is due on the first of the month. (Lease § 4)
- Deliver a written notice by hand to the office or by certified mail. It should describe the outage, say when you reported it, and state what you intend to do if it isn't fixed in 7 days. Keep a copy.

**Short answer:** Your lease doesn't give you a right to end it early. The manager's "no matter what" is still stronger than the law requires, because the landlord has to choose among several options if you leave.

**What the lease says.** I read the whole lease. It has no early-termination clause, no early-termination fee, and no addendum on liquidated damages. The term runs through "July 31, 2026" (§3). Section 10 says the lease can be changed only by a writing signed by both sides. So leaving on May 15 without the landlord's written agreement would be a breach.

**What the statute lets the landlord do.** Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595, if you surrender or abandon the unit, the landlord may choose one of these:
- **Subsection (1):** end the lease and retake the unit, which ends your liability.
- **Subsection (2):** retake the unit for your account and try to relet it. The landlord must use "good faith in attempting to relet," and any rent from a new tenant is deducted. You would owe only the shortfall.
- **Subsection (3):** "stand by and do nothing," holding you liable for rent as it comes due. This is the option that would match what the manager said, and it could mean rent through July.
- **Subsection (4):** charge an early-termination fee or liquidated damages. That is available only if you signed a separate addendum agreeing to it at the start. Your lease has none, so this option isn't open to the landlord.

So the manager could pursue rent through July under subsection (3), but that is one option and not the only one. If the landlord retakes the unit under subsection (2) or (1), you would owe less. I can't tell from what I have which option the landlord will pick.

**One exception.** Section 83.682 lets a tenant end a lease early without owing the remaining rent. As I read it, that applies to service members, and I don't know whether it covers you.

Are you, or is anyone on your lease, on active military duty or under military orders?

**What to do:** If you dispute the $500, object in writing within 15 days after you receive the letter. Don't wait to see whether the landlord sends the rest of your deposit first.

**Why**
- Under 83.49(3)(b), if you don't object within 15 days of receiving the notice, the landlord "may then deduct the amount of his or her claim." The landlord must then send you the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice.
- Missing the deadline isn't fatal. Under 83.49(3)(b), failing to object "does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." An objection still keeps your position much stronger.
- Your lease doesn't address deposit claims or objections. Section 7 says written notices to the landlord must be hand-delivered to the office (1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A) or sent there by certified mail. Send your objection that way, not by email. Keep a copy and your proof of delivery.
- The housing is not school housing, so Part II applies. That is the fact you confirmed.

**Your deadline:** I've noted that you received the letter today, but I can't count your 15 days until you confirm that date in the sidebar. Once you do, I'll give you the exact last day.

**Is the claim valid?** The statute doesn't say whether $500 for carpet cleaning is reasonable. That depends on the carpet's condition and what the landlord can show. The notice must also state the reason for the claim, and it must say the amount (83.49(3)(a)). Your objection can challenge the amount, the reason, or both.

**Does the letter satisfy the notice rule?** This is unsettled until I know how it was sent. The required notice is written notice "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.49(3)(a)). Your lease section 8 says the parties have not agreed to email notices.
- If it came by regular mail, it isn't the required form. On that reading, the landlord forfeits the claim and owes the full $1,050. The other reading is that a notice you actually received in time is enough, since 83.505(6) "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law."
- Timing is not a problem for the landlord. The 30 days from the lease end (July 31, 2026) run to 2026-08-30 and have not passed. Counted from your move-out (July 30, 2026), they run to 2026-08-29 and have not passed either.
- You moved out one day before the lease ended. Section 83.49(5) requires 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery before leaving early. Your email address notice wouldn't meet that. If no such notice was given, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day notice requirement. You would still keep your right to the deposit. That makes a forfeiture argument harder.

Either way, the landlord has to send you the remaining deposit, and your objection protects your right to dispute the $500. If either side sues over the deposit, the winner can recover court costs and a reasonable attorney fee (83.49(3)(c)).

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body" (83.49(4)).
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended. move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)).

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

answer:
Missing Thursday doesn't give you a legal remedy yet. Whether you have one depends on two things I can't confirm from here.

**1. Whether the landlord has to fix the AC at all (unsettled, and something you can check).**
- Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)5 lists "heat during winter, running water, and hot water." It doesn't list air conditioning.
- Under § 83.51(1)(a), the landlord must "comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes."
- So the question is whether Gainesville or Alachua County's housing code requires cooling, or a maximum indoor temperature. If it does, the broken AC is likely a § 83.51(1) violation. If it doesn't, the statute may not require him to repair it.
- Your lease doesn't help here. It has no clause on repairs or AC.
- You can check the local code. I can't look it up with my tools.

**2. Whether you've given the written notice the statute requires (probably not yet).**
- Under § 83.56(1), you can terminate only if the landlord materially fails to comply with § 83.51(1) "within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate."
- The 7 days start when that notice is delivered. They don't start when the AC broke or when the landlord missed Thursday.
- Lease § 7 says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or sent there "by certified mail."
- Lease § 8 says the parties "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail."
- Whether a text counts as written notice is unsettled. Section 83.56(4) lists mailing, delivering a copy, or e-mail under § 83.505. A text isn't on that list. A landlord could argue your text doesn't count. You could argue it's still writing he received.
- The safe route is a letter that follows lease § 7.

**What the remedies would be if a code violation is confirmed:**
- If the landlord still hasn't fixed it 7 days after proper notice, you could terminate.
- Under § 83.56(1)(a)–(b), if the failure is beyond his control and he keeps trying to fix it, you may owe reduced rent, or none if you move out because the unit is untenantable.
- Withholding rent is riskier. Section 83.60(1)(b) requires a separate 7-day written notice saying you intend not to pay rent. Don't withhold without that notice.

Besides the texts, have you hand-delivered or mailed anything in writing to the office at Suite A?

Probably not. The landlord is only partly right, though. You don't owe rent through July "no matter what."

**What your lease says.** The lease has no early-termination clause, no early-termination fee, and no liquidated-damages addendum. Nothing in it lets you end the tenancy early. **What the statute says.** If you leave and give up or abandon the unit, the landlord has to choose one of the remedies in § 83.595:

- **Subsection (2) is the landlord retaking possession "for the account of the tenant."** You would owe the rent under the lease minus what the landlord gets from re-renting the unit. The landlord must use good faith efforts to re-rent. Any rent from a new tenant must be deducted from what you owe.
- **Subsection (1) is the landlord treating the lease as ended.** That would end your liability. It is the landlord's choice, so don't count on it.

**What is unsettled.** The statute lists these remedies as the landlord's choices. So the landlord may be able to pick subsection (3) and not re-rent, and the statute does not clearly say otherwise. All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

answer:
**Thursday has passed with no repair.** Whether the delay is legally a problem depends on one thing I can't check: whether a local code requires cooling.

**Does the law require him to fix the AC?**
- The statute doesn't list AC. Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)5 requires "heat during winter, running water, and hot water," and says nothing about cooling.
- Section 83.51(1)(a) requires the landlord to "comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes." If Gainesville's housing code requires working cooling, a broken AC could fall under that. I can't look up local codes with my tools, so you would need to check Gainesville's housing code or ask the city code enforcement office.
- Your lease doesn't address AC or repair timing. Section 5 covers the deposit and §§ 7–8 cover notices, but nothing covers maintenance. So the lease gives you no repair deadline of its own.

**What you can do now**
- Under § 83.56(1), you may terminate the lease if the landlord materially fails to comply with § 83.51(1) within 7 days after he gets your written notice. The notice must describe the problem and say you intend to terminate because of it.
- If you would rather stay and stop paying rent, § 83.60(1)(b) requires a written notice saying you won't pay rent because of the noncompliance. The defense is available only after 7 days have passed. It only works if the court finds a material violation of § 83.51(1), which brings you back to the local-code question. If he sues for nonpayment, you would have to pay the rent into the court registry (§ 83.60(2)) or you could lose the defense. Withholding rent is risky if the code doesn't cover AC.
- If the cause is outside his control and he is making every reasonable effort, § 83.56(1)(a)–(b) says the rent for the period of noncompliance may be reduced in proportion to the lost rental value. If the unit is untenantable and you move out, you owe no rent while it stays that way.

**Your texts probably aren't enough.** Section 83.56(4) allows delivery by mailing, delivering a true copy, or e-mail under § 83.505. Your lease (§ 7) says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address. Section 8 says the parties haven't agreed to e-mail notices. Texting isn't on either list. The safest course is a written notice delivered by hand or sent by certified mail to Suite A. Keep a copy.
